item.title: Upgrading an off-grid shed: bigger battery, bigger panels
item.description: A small 12V solar setup in a shed gets a 200Ah battery and a pair of 260W panels — what's there now, what's changing, and why.
item.content:encoded:
The shed's power board as it stands today. Left to right: charge controller, fuse block with two USB/12V outlets, bus bars, inverter. (The yellow Sun King on the right is its own separate system.)

We're upgrading a small off-grid solar setup in a shed: swapping in a much bigger battery and adding a pair of full-size solar panels. It's a nice example of how a simple 12V system is put together — and of what needs to change when you scale one up. Here's what's there now, what's changing, and the reasoning behind each choice.

The current setup

The system is a classic small 12V layout: a solar panel feeds a charge controller, the controller charges a battery, and the battery feeds a fuse block that supplies the loads — a couple of USB/12V outlets and an inverter for 110V AC.

Part What it is What it does
Charge controller Renogy Rover 30A MPPT Takes power from the panel and charges the battery safely
Battery Dakota Lithium 12V 23Ah LiFePO4 (295 Wh) Stores energy for nights and cloudy days
Inverter Renogy 700W pure sine wave Turns 12V DC into 110V AC for ordinary plugs
Fuse block 6-way blade fuse block (5A, 7.5A, 30A fitted) Protects each circuit's wiring
Outlets Two panel-mount USB/12V sockets Phone and device charging
The wiring diagram taped up next to the board — panel → charge controller → battery → fuses → loads. Every system should have one of these posted!

The upgrade

A much bigger battery: 200Ah AGM

The new battery: a Renogy 12V 200Ah AGM deep-cycle battery.

The new battery is a Renogy 12V 200Ah AGM (absorbed glass mat — a sealed lead-acid battery). On paper it stores about 2,400 Wh, roughly eight times the old battery. In practice, lead-acid batteries last much longer if you only use about half their capacity, so the usable figure is closer to 1,200 Wh — still about four times what the shed has now.

Switching from lithium to AGM changes a few things:

  • The charge controller needs new settings. Lithium and lead-acid batteries want different charging voltages, so the Rover gets switched from its lithium profile to its sealed/AGM profile (and the voltages checked against the battery's label).
  • It's heavy — around 130 lb. It lives on the floor or a solid shelf, not on the wall.
  • It's better in the cold. Lithium batteries shouldn't be charged below freezing; AGMs can be, which matters in an unheated New England shed.
  • It likes to be kept full. Lead-acid batteries wear out when they sit partly discharged, so it's worth protecting them from deep discharge with a low-voltage cutoff set around 12.0V.
  • Old and new don't mix. The lithium battery comes out of this system entirely, rather than being wired alongside the AGM.

Two 260W solar panels, in series

The new panels: JA Solar 260W, standard 60-cell modules.

The panels are JA Solar 260W, standard 60-cell modules (37.98V open-circuit, 30.63V at max power, about 8.5A). Two of them, wired in series, are a good match for this charge controller and battery:

  • Voltage stays safely under the controller's limit. Two in series is about 76V open-circuit. Panel voltage rises in cold weather — maybe to the high 80s on a frigid January morning — which still leaves headroom under the controller's 100V input limit. Three in series would exceed it.
  • Current stays low (about 9A), so ordinary 10 AWG PV wire works fine even on a longer run to the shed.
  • A little oversizing is a feature. 520W of panels is a bit more than a 30A controller can pass into a 12V battery (about 400–430W). On bright summer days it simply caps out; on gray winter days the extra panel area means more charging than a smaller array would give.
  • Rough winter budget: about 0.8–1.2 kWh per day in December from the pair — enough to refill the battery's usable capacity in a day or two of decent sun.
  • Tilt them steeply. Around 55–60°, facing south, favors the low winter sun and sheds snow.

Making it safer as it gets bigger

A bigger battery can deliver a lot more current into a short circuit, so the protection gets an upgrade along with everything else:

  • A main fuse right at the battery's positive terminal, sized to the main cable.
  • A fuse between the charge controller and the battery (about 40A for a 30A controller).
  • A disconnect between the panels and the controller, rated for DC and at least 100V, so the array can be safely switched off.
  • Its own heavy cable and fuse for the inverter. A 700W inverter can pull around 65A from a 12V battery. Right now it shares the fuse block's 30A circuit, which caps it at roughly 350W. With the new battery it gets a dedicated cable and fuse straight from the bus bar, sized per the inverter's manual.
  • Grounded panel frames and racking.

And when swapping the battery: with this kind of controller, disconnect the panels first and reconnect them last — the controller needs to see the battery before it sees solar power.

What's next

Mounting the panels, running the cable into the shed, and swapping the battery. We'll post photos of the finished setup — and if you'd like to learn to build a system like this yourself, this is exactly the kind of thing we cover at our solar workshops.

item.title: Mesh radio with Rural Rivers
item.description: A low-cost, off-grid water-level sensor for community flood monitoring — built with the Rural Rivers project in Vermont.
item.content:encoded:
We're teaming up with the Rural Rivers / Mapping for Resilience project on low-cost, community-run flood monitoring.

Rural Rivers is a research-for-resilience effort — led by researchers at Dartmouth College and the Colorado School of Mines, working alongside flood-impacted communities in the Black and White River Valleys of rural Vermont, which have weathered repeated major floods over the past fifteen years. The project studies how communities respond to overlapping crises, and how clearer communication and better information can strengthen local resilience.

Timely information about how high the water is getting is a big part of that picture — and it's exactly what our water-level sensor is designed to provide.

The sensor is a MeshCore-based ultrasonic water-level monitor: an ultrasonic rangefinder measures the distance down to the water's surface, and the reading is relayed over LoRa mesh radio — so it keeps reporting even where there's no cell service or internet. It's inexpensive to build, can run on solar, and is designed to be set up by anyone.

If you'd like to build and configure one, everything you need is on the configuration page for the water-level sensor → — flash the firmware, pair the two devices, and connect to WiFi, right from your browser.

item.title: Meetup with Goodwin Hill Goats
item.description: A conversation about the ways kids learn with — and from — other animals.
item.content:encoded: Halé and I met up at pasture to talk about ways of weaving WFS curricula into activities that would support Goodwin Hill Goats: helping with feeding and care of the goats, foraging for supplemental goat greens, and helping with infrastructure upkeep and repair. Looking forward to more brainstorming soon!

item.title: Toaster-oven reflow at Artisans Asylum
item.description: Testing toaster-oven reflow-soldering techniques at Artisans Asylum.
item.content:encoded: Testing out toaster-oven soldering techniques at Artisans Asylum with Mike; with a little bit of tweaking, we were able to get both ovens set up nicely, allowing for parallel surface mount soldering of small boards! Looking to use this technique to make more blinky boards and radio nodes soon …

item.title: Sailing and STEM with the Edgewood Sailing School
item.description: Meeting with the Edgewood Sailing School to scope STEM workshops for 2026 — mesh radio, a dock-mounted water-level sensor, and more.
item.content:encoded: Craig and I met up with Ben and Alex of Edgewood Sailing School to brainstorm about various STEM workshop ideas for their 2026 Sailing School, including an introduction to mesh radio. We're also planning on setting up a water level sensor on the dock, sending its data via mesh radio to the internet. More soon!

item.title: Girl Scouts "Intro to Solar Power" at West Medford
item.description: An Intro to Solar Power workshop with a Girl Scout troop at the West Medford Community Center.
item.content:encoded: An "Intro to Solar Power" workshop for a Girl Scout troop at the West Medford Community Center — what a fun day! We used simple voltmeters to measure solar panel voltages, and then wired up two solar panels in series to power a small motor. We also experimented with LEDs and coin cell batteries, and used a 'nibbler' (a drill with an attachment that can safely cut thin sheet material), powered by a larger solar panel, to cut custom shapes out of cardboard. We're planning more meetups soon!

item.title: Designing a Supercapacitor Battery Model
item.description: Designing a simple supercapacitor circuit that models battery charging and discharging on a fast, observable timescale — and doubles as a crank-powered flashlight for workshops.
item.content:encoded:
Mike suggested that we could make a simple circuit where a supercapacitor serves as a quick-to-charge, quick-to-discharge battery. This would let us easily measure changes in voltage and current during charging and discharging on a reasonable timescale — something that's hard to observe with conventional batteries, which take hours to cycle.

Because supercapacitors can be charged and discharged virtually unlimited times without degradation, they make an ideal hands-on model for exploring how batteries work. The setup could also double as a practical device: a small crank-powered flashlight, using a DC motor as a generator to charge the supercapacitor.

We'll be designing the circuit soon and using it in upcoming workshops.
